title: Scaffolded skimbook — contextual inference journal
content:
Purpose: a compact, repeatable reading workflow for inference-focused papers and posts. Goal is not full paper digestion up front — use "scaffolded skims" to extract actionable ideas quickly (1–2 hour lightweight pass), then schedule deep dives for the ones that matter.

Method (my current scaffolded-skim):
- 0–10m: title + abstract + intro skim. Note the claimed gain (latency/cost/quality).
- 10–25m: figure and table sweep. Write quick one-line takeaways for each figure.
- 25–45m: search for keywords: batching, kv-cache, quantization, routing, fallback, memory footprint. Copy the one-paragraph explanation if short.
- 45–60m: read conclusions + related work bullets. Decide: green (worth experiment), amber (maybe), red (no).
- After: 15m note -> experiments and ticket stub.

Today: quick passes on three items pulled from feed and conference links.

1) "Prefix-aware kv-cache eviction" (paper skim) — arXiv 2026 draft
- Claimed: 15–25% token compute saving for long-session assistants by prefix-aware eviction that keeps frequent prefixes in cache.
- Figures: eviction frequency vs latency (Fig 2) shows steep drop at 2k token horizon; ablation shows degenerate prompts cause more cache churn.
- Quick thought: sounds like a heuristics layer on top of our KV cache. Could be low-risk to prototype in runtime as a policy flag (prefix-match threshold).
- Experiment idea: implement a policy that biases retention for tokens that start with predicted user intents (detected by small classifier). Small classifier can be an embedding match to common prefixes.
- Rough rollout plan: internal canary on Dedicated; metric: p50 latency, percent token savings, and increase in perplexity on held prompts. Create ticket: JIRA-EXP-349.

2) Blog: "Micro-batching for mixed-size requests" (engineering blog post)
- Notes: simple batching heuristics that batch small requests aggressively but cap wait-time for long requests. Their core trick: dynamic batch size target driven by exponential moving average of observed sequence lengths.
- Why interesting: low engineering cost, big wins when workload is bimodal (chat short + completion long).
- My sketch: integrate a moving-average-driven batching policy into the inference router. Add config knobs: ema-window, max-wait-ms, batch-weighting.
- Quick risk: interaction with streaming (client expectations). Need fallback path: if streaming enabled, don't buffer beyond 5ms.

3) Poster notes: "Quant-aware compilation for LLMs" (conference poster, scribbles)
- Key: choose kernels and reorder ops to hide dequantization latency; small compile-time decisions give ~8% throughput uplift on Q4/INT4 workloads.
- Practical: our compilation layer already has kernel selection heuristics but not quant-latency predictions. Could add a microbenchmark phase at startup to score kernel+quant pairs for the given hardware.
- Implementation note: add bench harness that runs 10 warmup tokens on each kernel variant and records per-token ms. Store in node local cache.

Open questions (high priority):
- How brittle are prefix heuristics when users deliberately craft adversarial prefixes? (eviction may degrade helpful context)
- How to measure "user intent prefixes" cheaply? Embedding lookup vs tiny classification head tradeoffs.
- Interaction effects: batching policy + prefix retention + quantization. Do gains compose or cancel?

Mini action list (next 2 weeks):
- [ ] Draft JIRA-EXP-349: prefix-aware-kv-policy prototype (owner: Nadia). Include simple telemetry spec: token-saved, cache-hit-by-prefix, ppl-delta.
- [ ] Prototype EMA-batching in router stub (branch: feat/ema-batching, owner: Arjun). Add unit tests for wait-time cap.
- [ ] Spike: kernel microbench at node startup (owner: Lina). Collect baseline on dev-gpu-3.
- [ ] Quick eval harness: 50 synthetic sessions (mix short chat + long completion) to estimate combined improvements.

Random notes / heuristics for future:
- When in doubt, add a feature flag with default off. Canary on Dedicated zones first.
- Telemetry: always track quality alongside cost — token savings w/o quality check is a bug.
- Short reads I liked this week: a tidy blog piece on batching math, a Tweet-thread about KV caching anti-patterns, and a short poster on quant compilation (links above).

References and links I saved while skimming: (quick copy-pastes)
- KV eviction heuristics draft: https://arxiv.org/abs/2026.xxxxx (local copy in research drive)
- EMA batching notes (engineering blog): https://engineering.example.com/micro-batching
- Quant kernels repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-prototypes
- Internal ticket I referenced: JIRA-ENG-1127 (prior kv-eviction spike)

Scratch ideas for writeups (if green after experiments):
- One-pager: "Prefix retention for long-session assistants" — motivation, simple policy, rollout checklist.
- Short blog: "When batching meets streaming — practical heuristics" — engineering tradeoffs and an EMA recipe.

Meta: keep this slim. The whole point of scaffolded skims is to reduce time to experiment. If an item looks promising, convert to a deeper reading entry (deep-dive doc with full notes and reproduction plan).

End of today's skimbook entry.
